title: Seneca's rehearsal
hookLine: rehearse losses ahead of time so they don't ambush you (Letters 91)

lines: A CITY BURNS IN ONE NIGHT.
THINK OF IT BEFORE IT HAPPENS.
cards: News reached Rome that the city of Lugdunum, today's Lyon in France, had burned to the ground. A prosperous, handsome city, gone in a single night.
Seneca had a friend from Lugdunum named Liberalis, and Liberalis was devastated, not only by the loss but by the shock of it. He had never seen it coming.

Seneca wrote about it in a letter to another friend, Lucilius, describing a practice that can soften a blow like that. It sounds strange at first: think about disasters on purpose, before they happen.

teach.b: Premeditatio means thinking ahead. Modern writers often add malorum: premeditatio malorum, thinking ahead about hard things. Cicero discusses the idea too, in his Tusculan Disputations.
In Letter 91, Seneca says, in paraphrase, that nothing should be unexpected by us.
Send the mind out ahead to meet everything that could happen, not only what usually happens but what can. Exile, illness, war, shipwreck. The blow that's been foreseen, he says, lands lighter.
What hurts most is the ambush: the loss that arrives when we'd assumed it never could. This can sound like a recipe for anxiety, so here's what it is not. It isn't worrying.
Worry replays the same fear over and over, with no end and no plan. Seneca's rehearsal is short and deliberate.

teach.h: NOT WORRY: ONCE, CALMLY, THEN BACK.
teach.b: You picture a loss, calmly, once. You notice that you could survive it, and what you'd do. Then you come back to today and notice the loss hasn't happened.
Your job is still here. Your friend is still alive. The city is still standing.
Modern Stoic writers such as William Irvine call this negative visualization, and they stress that return: the rehearsal makes what you have look less guaranteed, and so more precious.
Seneca's version came out of a real fire, in a real city, and a friend in grief.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism use a brief rehearsal of possible losses, following Seneca's Letter 91, picturing a setback calmly and then returning to what they still have.

o: planning a wrong in advance, as in law
thinking ahead about losses, calmly, once
dwelling on every fear before it comes

games.q: what's inside the rehearsal — tap the pairs.
p: today's Lyon, burned in one night
the loss we assumed could never come

s: Seneca's rehearsal is the same as worrying
worry loops with no end. the rehearsal is short, calm, once, and then you come back.
Seneca wrote Letter 91 after a whole city burned in one night
Lugdunum, today's Lyon, and his friend Liberalis was devastated.
the practice is meant to make you expect the worst all day
you picture a loss once, then return and notice what you still have.

games.q: you're Seneca. your friend Liberalis is shattered because his city burned without warning. what do you write about it to your friend Lucilius?
o: it was bad luck; try to forget it.
nothing should be unexpected: send the mind ahead to meet what can happen.
cities always burn eventually; don't be upset.
games.why: he writes that the blow foreseen lands lighter, and the mind should go out ahead to meet what can happen, not only what usually does.

practice: Keep it small today: picture losing something minor, your phone, a favorite mug, a day's plans canceled, and see it happen, calmly. Notice that you would manage, and you'd know what to do.
Then come back, the phone still here, the mug still on the shelf, and let the picture go, glad of the ordinary thing that's still yours.

wordCard.voice: Premeditatio. Latin for thinking ahead: rehearsing losses briefly, so they don't ambush you. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: thinking ahead, rehearsing in the mind. The full phrase praemeditatio malorum means thinking ahead about hard things.

carryVoice: Your line: foreseen is lighter. It's the ambush that hurts most. That's day one hundred twenty-six.

sources.ref: Letters 91 (to Lucilius, on Liberalis and the burning of Lugdunum)
